data_mart_framing.headline: This sz_dm_* SQL schema is ONE illustrative, intentionally oversized proof-of-concept example — NOT the required or canonical way to report on Senzing. Many teams need NO mart at all; most who do need only a simple one.
data_mart_framing.do_you_need_a_mart: First decide whether you need a mart at all — often you do not. Real-time risk or value scoring, entity graphs, and how/why explanations can all be answered by querying Senzing directly on the affected entities (get_entity, why, how, find_network/find_path), with no extra storage to build or keep in sync. Build a mart only to serve queries Senzing itself cannot, or at a scale or latency that needs a separate store — and then build the smallest one that does the job.
typical_answers: No mart at all (most common). Query Senzing directly on the affected entities for real-time risk/value analysis, entity graphs (find_network/find_path), and how/why explanations. Nothing extra to build or keep in sync.

A simple entity map kept in a lightweight store (covers most who DO need a mart). For example: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch with one JSON document per entity; a data lake with an entity-to-record map for joins; or a key-value store (Redis, DynamoDB). Add a graph database (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune) when you need graph analytics that combine resolved entities with data Senzing does not resolve, such as transactions and events.

A heavier analytical mart — like the sz_dm_* SQL example (its full schema is returned by the data_mart topic), or a full database server such as PostgreSQL — ONLY when you genuinely need rich pre-aggregated reporting and insight statistics (for example a POC showcase). This is the least common case. Size it to what you actually query.
data_mart_framing.what_it_is: The sz_dm_* SQL example — the schema the data_mart topic returns, and the tables that the SQL queries here reference — is that least-common case: one example the Senzing MCP server can build. It deliberately includes far more tables and statistics than a real deployment needs — a broad POC showcase (examples, visualization, reporting, insights, statistics) — so treat it as a starting sketch, not a specification. These sz_dm_* tables do not exist unless you choose to build them.
warnings: This is NOT a Senzing product and NOT part of the Senzing SDK. It does not exist out of the box. The sz_dm_ prefix makes it LOOK like an official Senzing product; it is not — the prefix is only used in this example.

This is NOT a required design. You may not need any mart. If you do need one, it can be non-SQL. Nothing here — the SQL engine, the sz_dm_ prefix, or the table and column names — is a standard to copy.
This is NOT how a real deployment should be sized. This example is oversized on purpose; a real mart is usually much smaller — build only the data your reporting and access patterns actually need.
data_mart_framing.guidance: Start by asking whether a mart is needed at all; if not, just use Senzing. If one is needed, prefer a simple entity map in a store that fits your business needs and technology stack, and build only what your reporting and access patterns require. For a POC, using this SQL example verbatim is fine and expected; otherwise do not inherit its engine, schema, or table names by default.

design_concepts.name: Precision, Recall, and F1 for Entity Resolution
design_concepts.description: When a truth set (known correct entity assignments) is available, measure ER accuracy using pairwise metrics. Precision = correct resolved pairs / total resolved pairs (how many matches are correct?). Recall = correct resolved pairs / total true pairs (how many true matches did we find?). F1 = 2 * (P * R) / (P + R) (balanced accuracy). High precision with low recall means conservative resolution (few false positives but missing matches). Low precision with high recall means aggressive resolution (catching more matches but with false positives). The sz_audit tool computes these automatically from a truth set CSV.
computes: Precision: correct pairs / total resolved pairs
Recall: correct pairs / total true pairs
F1 score: harmonic mean of precision and recall

design_concepts.name: Split and Merge Detection
design_concepts.description: Comparing current resolution against a truth set reveals two error types. Splits (false negatives): records that should be in the same entity but are separated across multiple resolved entities. Merges (false positives): records from different real-world entities that are incorrectly combined into one resolved entity. Each split/merge can be drilled down by match key to understand what caused the error, enabling targeted configuration tuning. Splits suggest missing features or overly strict rules. Merges suggest generic features (common names) or overly permissive rules. The sz_audit tool identifies both automatically.
computes: Split count: entities in truth set that span multiple resolved entities
Merge count: resolved entities that contain records from multiple truth entities
Split/merge drill-down by match key and ER rule

design_concepts.name: Review Queue and Sampling Strategies
design_concepts.description: Quality assessment requires reviewing specific entities, not just aggregate statistics. Build review queues from: (1) possible matches — entity pairs that almost resolved but lacked sufficient evidence, (2) ambiguous matches — records with conflicting signals, (3) large entities — those exceeding a size threshold that may indicate over-matching, (4) entities with review features — entities where a feature type appears more than once (e.g., two different DOBs or SSNs). For large datasets, use random stratified sampling: sample N entities from each size bucket and each cross-source combination. This gives representative coverage without reviewing every entity. Document sample size and selection criteria for reproducibility.
steps: Define review criteria: possible matches, ambiguous matches, large entities, multi-valued features
Build priority-ordered queues from direct SDK calls and export output — or, if you built a mart, from queries against it
For large populations, use stratified random sampling (N per size bucket per source pair)
Use why_entities to investigate each flagged entity pair
Document findings and track resolution quality over time

sql_patterns.name: entity_size_breakdown
sql_patterns.description: Distribution of records per entity — how many entities have 1, 2, 3-5, 6-10, 11-50, or 51+ records.
notes: Singletons (1 record) are unmatched records — may indicate data quality issues or unique records.
Entities with 51+ records should be reviewed for potential over-matching.

sql_patterns.name: large_entity_review
sql_patterns.description: Entities with more records than a threshold — potential over-matching candidates.
notes: Adjust the threshold (10) based on your data — for some datasets, 5+ is suspicious.
Use why_entities or how_entity SDK calls to investigate specific large entities.
GROUP_CONCAT syntax varies by database — use STRING_AGG in PostgreSQL.

sql_patterns.name: possible_match_queue
sql_patterns.description: Possible matches for analyst review — entity pairs that almost resolved together.
notes: PM = Possibly Same (strong but not conclusive match — not enough evidence to auto-resolve).
These are candidates for human review or additional data enrichment.
Match types: AM = Ambiguous Match, PM = Possibly Same, DR = Disclosed Relation, PR = Possible Relation.

sql_patterns.name: ambiguous_match_queue
sql_patterns.description: Ambiguous matches needing more evidence — entity pairs with conflicting signals.
notes: AM = Ambiguous Match (conflicting evidence — some features match, others conflict).
Typically requires domain expertise or additional data to resolve.
Match types: AM = Ambiguous Match, PM = Possibly Same, DR = Disclosed Relation, PR = Possible Relation.

sql_patterns.name: entity_size_anomalies
sql_patterns.description: Detect entity size distribution anomalies — entities significantly larger than the median, indicating potential over-matching.
notes: Entities 5x or more above the average size are strong candidates for over-matching review.
Use why_entities or how_entity to investigate the match chain of flagged entities.
Adjust the multiplier (5) based on domain expectations.

sql_patterns.name: cross_source_match_rate
sql_patterns.description: Match rate between each data source pair — what percentage of entities from source A also appear in source B.
notes: Match rate percentages reveal data source overlap quality.
Very high rates (>80%) may indicate duplicate data sources.
Very low rates (<1%) may indicate poor feature overlap or data quality issues.

sql_patterns.name: review_features
sql_patterns.description: Entities with multiple values for the same feature type — potential over-matching indicators.
notes: Review features are features that appear more than once in an entity.
Multiple addresses or phone numbers are often normal; multiple SSNs or DOBs are suspicious.
Use how_entity to see the step-by-step merge sequence and identify which record introduced the conflict.

sql_patterns.name: singleton_analysis
sql_patterns.description: Analyze unmatched (singleton) records by data source — high singleton rates may indicate data quality problems.
notes: High singleton rate (>90%) suggests poor matching features or low data overlap.
Compare singleton rates across sources — sources with similar data should have similar rates.
Singletons are not inherently bad — unique records naturally remain singletons.

visualization.name: entity_size_histogram
visualization.description: Bar chart showing the distribution of entity sizes (records per entity) — reveals deduplication patterns and potential over-matching.

visualization.name: precision_recall_scatter
visualization.description: Scatter plot of precision vs recall across configuration variants or data source pairs — reveals the accuracy trade-off and highlights where tuning is needed.
visualization.data_source: sz_audit output or truth set comparison

visualization.name: singleton_rate_by_source
visualization.description: Bar chart comparing singleton rates across data sources — high rates may indicate data quality issues or missing matching features.

anti_patterns.pattern: Measuring ER accuracy without a truth set
anti_patterns.correct: Precision, recall, and F1 require a truth set with known correct entity assignments. Without one, use proxy indicators: entity size distribution, cross-source match rates, review features, and manual sampling of possible matches. Proxy indicators reveal problems but cannot measure absolute accuracy.

anti_patterns.pattern: Only checking aggregate statistics for quality
anti_patterns.correct: Aggregate stats (entity count, compression ratio) hide errors. Always sample and manually review specific entities — especially large entities, possible matches, and ambiguous matches. Use why_entities to understand individual resolution decisions.

anti_patterns.pattern: Ignoring entity size distribution as a quality signal
anti_patterns.correct: Entity size distribution is the single best proxy for ER quality. Unexpectedly large entities signal over-matching (merges). Too many singletons signal under-matching (splits). Monitor the distribution continuously and investigate outliers.
